title: By the River
focus: despair and renewal by the river

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha reaches the river and, sick of himself, leans to drown. From deep within comes the sacred word Om, and he falls into a deep sleep under a coconut tree. He wakes renewed; Govinda, now a monk, has watched over him without recognizing him. Siddhartha reflects that he had to experience despair to learn its emptiness, and decides to stay by the river.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Now, Siddhartha smiled” slowly and put it in my own words: Govinda, now a monk, has watched over a sleeping stranger and does not recognize him; when he asks how the stranger knows his name, Siddhartha smiles. Next, craft. I notice the line is only four words, set alone after the monk's puzzled question, so the smile answers him before any words do. The strongest word is “smiled”: the smile is the first calm, knowing gesture after his despair at the river, so it marks a man who has come back to himself. Then, effect. Why does Siddhartha smile when the monk asks how he knows his name? My answer: Siddhartha has just been reborn by the river; he recognizes his old friend and is amused that Govinda cannot see him, which shows how completely the rich, tired Siddhartha has been left behind.

Next, craft. I notice the line is only four words, set alone after the monk's puzzled question, so the smile answers him before any words do. The strongest word is “smiled”: the smile is the first calm, knowing gesture after his despair at the river, so it marks a man who has come back to himself. Then, effect. Why does Siddhartha smile when the monk asks how he knows his name? My answer: Siddhartha has just been reborn by the river; he recognizes his old friend and is amused that Govinda cannot see him, which shows how completely the rich, tired Siddhartha has been left behind.

Exemplar: Siddhartha's despair at the river becomes the condition for his rebirth. When the text says “Deeply, he had been entangled in Sansara, he had sucked up disgust and death from all sides into his body, like a sponge sucks up water until it is full” (By the River, paragraph 1), it shows this directly. Full of Sansara "like a sponge sucks up water until it is full," he wants to die, but after the Om and his sleep "Siddhartha smiled," and he judges even his years in the city as a necessary part of the path.
